statements: The chief complaint is progressive right forearm, hand, and shoulder swelling and pain.
The patient ultimately presented with signs concerning for acute compartment syndrome of the right forearm/hand.
The key diagnostic task is to determine the underlying cause of this acute limb process.
Salient positive findings strongly support a crystal-induced inflammatory process complicated by compartment syndrome.
He has a known history of crystal-proven gout.
He has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes.
He is a young Polynesian man.
He has severe obesity with a BMI of 42.6.
These factors increase gout risk.
The symptoms began after light weight exercise.
The symptoms progressed over several days.
The swelling and pain were not relieved by his usual oral anti-inflammatories.
On exam he had tense volar forearm compartments.
On exam he had reduced finger sensation.
On exam he had decreased capillary refill.
On exam he had severe pain with passive finger stretch.
These are classic clinical features of compartment syndrome.
Measured pressures were elevated.
The measured pressures were especially 45–48 mm Hg in the carpal tunnel and palm.
The elevated pressures confirmed the compartment syndrome physiology.
Imaging showed fluid in the olecranon bursa.
Imaging showed fluid in the elbow joint.
Elbow aspiration demonstrated monosodium urate crystals.
Elbow aspiration demonstrated a very high synovial white-cell count.
Intraoperatively small tophi were seen in the flexor tendon synovial sheaths.
There was no pus at surgery.
There was no odor at surgery.
There was no necrotic muscle at surgery.
The muscles were still contractile.
These findings argue against necrotizing infection or ischemic muscle death as the primary process.
Wrist aspiration showed calcium pyrophosphate crystals.
Wrist aspiration showed no bacterial growth.
These findings further support crystal arthropathy rather than infection.
He was afebrile.
Blood toxicology was negative.
CT angiogram excluded vascular causes.
Doppler ultrasound excluded vascular causes.
MRI of the shoulder was unremarkable.
There was no bacterial growth from aspirated fluid.
Intraoperatively there was no pus.
Intraoperatively there was no foul odor.
CK was only mildly elevated at 245 U/L.
This does not support major rhabdomyolysis as the main driver.
Erythema could suggest cellulitis or septic arthritis.
Leukocytosis could suggest cellulitis or septic arthritis.
The absence of fever, negative cultures, and direct visualization without purulence make infection less likely as the primary diagnosis.
The leading differential is acute gout flare causing marked inflammatory swelling and tophaceous tenosynovial involvement, leading to acute compartment syndrome.
This fits the prior crystal-proven gout.
This fits monosodium urate crystals in the elbow aspirate.
This fits visible tophi in flexor tendon sheaths.
This fits the severe localized swelling with elevated compartment pressures.
A second consideration is septic arthritis/cellulitis with secondary compartment syndrome.
This is plausible because of erythema.
This is plausible because of leukocytosis.
This is plausible because of diabetes.
This is plausible because of a synovial WBC of 91,650/mm3.
However, the patient was afebrile.
However, cultures showed no bacterial growth.
However, surgery found no pus, odor, or necrosis.
Crystal arthritis can itself produce very high synovial WBC counts.
The evidence favors gout over infection.
Another consideration is exertional muscle injury/rhabdomyolysis causing swelling and compartment syndrome after exercise.
The exercise was described as light.
CK elevation was only mild.
The crystal findings and tophi provide a much more direct explanation.
CPPD could also be considered because wrist aspiration showed calcium pyrophosphate crystals.
His established gout history supports gout.
Monosodium urate crystals were found in the elbow.
Intraoperative tophi were seen.
CPPD may coexist.
CPPD is less likely to explain the full presentation.
The patient clearly had acute compartment syndrome of the right forearm/hand.

The underlying disease process most strongly supported by the case data is an acute gout flare with tophaceous flexor tenosynovitis producing enough inflammatory edema to precipitate compartment syndrome.
The crystal confirmation, tophi seen intraoperatively, and lack of evidence for infection or vascular injury make this the most likely diagnosis.
The differential diagnosis includes acute gout flare with tophaceous flexor tenosynovitis causing acute compartment syndrome.
The differential diagnosis includes septic arthritis/cellulitis with secondary compartment syndrome.
The differential diagnosis includes calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease flare.
The differential diagnosis includes exertional rhabdomyolysis or muscle injury causing compartment syndrome.
The final diagnosis is acute gout flare causing right forearm and hand compartment syndrome.
